paper_title: WorldBridge: Bridging Scattered Views for Coherent 3D World Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.

Introduction Creating explorable 3D worlds from images [29, 66, 97] has been long-standing challenge in computer vision, with broad applications in robotics [43], AR/VR [37], and video games [62]. In practical scenarios, users may wish to create 3D world from only few reference images, which can depict different parts of scene, exhibit substantially different visual appearances, and share little or no visual overlap. Such sparse observations leave large portions of scene unobserved, making its geometry and appearance underconstrained [55, 79]. Rather than treating such ambiguity solely as reconstruction challenge, we view it as an opportunity for controllable world generation, where users can specify how scattered references are spatially arranged while allowing unobserved regions to be plausibly synthesized. Yet, achieving this goal requires integrating scattered visual references, user-specified constraints, and generated content into spatially coherent 3D world. Existing methods have made considerable progress in 3D world generation. Imageand video-based approaches [8, 19, 98, 102] use powerful generative models to synthesize realistic views under camera control. However, these approaches may produce inconsistent 3D geometry across the generated views. Geometry-aware generative methods [20, 27, 34, 52] incorporate geometric information to improve the consistency of generated appearance and scene structure. Other approaches [61, 101] maintain geometric memories to preserve information from previously observed or generated views. Despite these advances, existing methods still struggle when the reference images have little or no visual overlap. Geometric information from isolated observations provides limited guidance for connecting distant regions, while generative models may introduce content that does not faithfully follow the input references. Consequently, maintaining both global scene coherence and reference fidelity remains difficult, particularly under flexible camera and text conditioning. In this work, we present WorldBridge, generative framework for creating coherent and controllable 3D worlds from scattered reference images with little or no visual overlap. We aim to preserve the observed content while plausibly generating the unseen regions under flexible camera and text conditioning. We coordinate shared global scene context with information from individual reference images. The global context ensures the consistent generation of geometry and appearance across different views. The individual references provide constraints to preserve the observed content. This allows us to generate plausible 3D worlds while maintaining consistency with the observations. This mechanism allows both types of references to be used without assigning artificial temporal positions to spatial references. plug-and-play latentreference consistency strategy further improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. Together, these designs enable us to generate both RGB images and 3D geometry for the requested camera viewpoints. Fig. 1 illustrates the capabilities of WorldBridge under different camera and text conditioning. First, WorldBridge can generate plausible 3D scene from scattered views with little overlap; see Fig. 1(a). As illuminated in Fig. 1(b), our method can also generate different spatial layouts from the same reference images by changing the camera poses. As Fig. 1(c) shows, we further allow users to control unseen regions through text prompts while preserving the observed content. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 1(d), our method generalizes well to references with markedly different visual styles, generating coherent 3D worlds even from combinations of real-world photographs and stylized images. To comprehensively verify our effectiveness around 3D world generation with scattered references, we introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite. Existing benchmarks [48, 103] focus on evaluating generation on overlapping reference views, while our benchmark provides up to six scattered references with little or no visual overlap. Specifically, WorldBridge-Short evaluates RGB synthesis from two low-overlap references in short real-world sequences of small scenes. WorldBridge-Long evaluates visual quality, geometric consistency, camera control, and reference fidelity using multiple low-overlap references in large real-world scenes. WorldBridge-Agent extends these evaluations to synthetic scenes, assessing the integration of both temporal references along the target trajectory and spatial references outside it. Extensive experiments on existing novel-view-synthesis benchmarks and our proposed WorldBridge benchmark demonstrate superior view fidelity, geometric accuracy, camera controllability, consistency, and generation quality, compared with previous approaches. To summarize, our contributions are listed as follows: We introduce WorldBridge, framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation from scattered images with little or no visual overlap. It preserves observations while plausibly generating unseen regions for 3D worlds through flexible camera and text conditioning. We propose coordinated generation strategy that combines global scene context with reference-specific information. Global-context-grounded generation provides shared guidance across views, while temporal and spatial reference attention integrates temporal and spatial references without requiring them to share temporal positions. plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy further improves reference fidelity. We introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite, comprising short, long, and agent-based settings, assessing reference fidelity, geometric consistency, and camera control under low-overlap and onand off-trajectory conditions of 3D world generation. 2. Related Work Novel View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction. Novel view synthesis (NVS) generates images from unseen viewpoints using reference observations. Optimization-based methods [1, 36, 53, 54] reconstruct implicit or explicit 3D representations from posed images for photorealistic rendering. Sparse-view methods [13, 33, 55, 70, 90, 104] use regularization to improve reconstruction from limited observations. Feed-forward methods [3, 4, 7, 41, 67, 71, 74 76, 82, 92, 95] further leverage learned multi-view and geometric priors to recover 3D representations from sparse or unposed images, with motion and structure priors also supporting robust monocular depth estimation under adverse conditions [86]. Generative methods synthesize plausible content beyond the observed regions, drawing on image and video diffusion priors for novel view synthesis [6, 8, 19, 45, 60, 61, 79, 80, 98, 101, 102] and learned geometric priors for 3D shape completion [87]. Recent geometry-aware methods [20, 21, 27, 34, 35, 52, 77, 83] incorporate geometric representations or model appearance and geometry jointly to improve 3D consistency, with related cross-modal alignment challenges arising in joint audiovideo generation [84]. concurrent work [40] leverages camera-queried implicit representations for end-to-end novel view synthesis. In contrast, our work focuses on the more unconstrained setting of bridging scattered onand off-trajectory references with little or no visual overlap to generate coherent 3D worlds. 3D Scene Generation. Research on 3D content spans spatiotemporal reasoning over dynamic point clouds [100] and the generation of diverse, explorable environments. Early methods [9, 46, 91] use learned scene representations and compositional priors to generate large-scale environments. Other methods [10, 44, 65, 99] leverage pretrained image generators for textand image-conditioned scene synthesis. Recent approaches [16, 32, 39, 51, 69, 78, 96, 97] support scene expansion and interactive exploration, with multi-agent workflows also used for scientific video understanding [85] and for spatially consistent video generation across clips using shared 3D layouts [64]. Cameracontrolled methods [12, 29, 63, 66] further enable exploration along specified camera trajectories. While these approaches advance controllable world generation, integrating multiple scattered observations is not their primary focus. WorldBridge instead generates coherent 3D worlds from multiple posed references with little or no overlap, including references outside the target camera trajectory. It coordinates shared scene context with individual reference information to guide generation while preserving observed content. 3. Proposed Method 3.1. Preliminaries Geometry Autoencoder. Baselines. We compare our method against comprehensive set of recent scene generation approaches [8, 27, 34, 52, 77, 102], including the view-based generative methods and the scene-query-based methods. All generative methods are evaluated under their official settings, while ours uses 50 denoising steps and classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale of 2. For prior methods, we align the scale of the camera trajectory to their proper scale; for [8], we align the geometry from Pi3 [76] to the given cameras scale and do reprojection with aligned geometry and the given camera. Differences in supported reference configurations and inference procedures are detailed in the supplementary material. Evaluation Datasets and Metrics. We assess all methods on the public novel-view-synthesis benchmarks and our proposed WorldBridge benchmark suite. The public NVS benchmarks include RealEstate10K [103] and DL3DV [48], both including 100 1-view and 100 2-view samples, and we follow the evaluation split of [105]. Experiments on public NVS benchmarks and our WorldBridge-Short focus on novel view generation fidelity, assessing PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. Experiments on WorldBridge-Long and WorldBridge-Agent target assessing camera controllability (ATE and rotational and translational RPE), scene consistency (feature and geometric reprojection errors), reference fidelity (reference-to-target reprojection LPIPS), and generation quality (aesthetic score). The evaluation of camera control and consistency utilizes the geometry estimated from VGGT-Ω [73]. As WorldBridge-Long contains the labels for captured RGB images and estimated depth annotations, we also assess the novel view fidelity and geometry accuracy (AbsRel, δ1). More details are listed in the supp. 4.3. Quantitative Results Tables 14 evaluate quantitative results on different benchmarks. Ours achieves the best RGB fidelity on RealEstate10K and DL3DV under oneand two-view settings (Tab. 1). On the low-overlap WorldBridge-Short, it improves PSNR from 16.13 to 18.35 dB over the best baseline (Tab. 2), demonstrating effective sparse-reference integration. For long-range generation, Ours improves PSNR from 16.43 to 17.68 dB and reduces AbsRel against estimated depth from 0.454 to 0.345 compared with GLD, while achieving the lowest geometric reprojection error (Tab. 3). On WorldBridge-Agent, it achieves the lowest camera-pose and geometric reprojection errors with both onand off-trajectory references (Tab. 4), supporting flexible reference conditioning. 4.4. Applications As shown in Fig. 1, WorldBridge reconstructs scenes from sparse references and controls their layout via reference camera poses. Text prompts guide the content of unseen regions, while combining real and stylized references enables imaginative world generation. More visualizations are provided in the supplementary material. 5. Removing the global scene branch lowers PSNR on WorldBridge-Long from 17.68 to 16.61 dB and more than doubles geometric reprojection error on Agent Off, from 0.061 to 0.126. With the scene branch retained, removing its RGB supervision (Lsc) lowers Long PSNR from 17.68 to 17.18 dB and increases reference error in all three settings. Training with both temporal and spatial references yields lower reference error than training with either type alone on Long, Agent On/Off. The difference is largest on Agent Off, where reference error is 0.344 with mixed training, compared with 0.391 with temporal references alone and 0.368 with spatial references alone. LRC raises PSNR from 17.30 to 17.68 dB and lowers reference error in all settings, with reduction from 0.361 to 0.344 on Agent Off. 6. Conclusion We present WorldBridge, which generates coherent 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no overlap. Global scene context guides each view, while temporal and spatial reference attention preserves observed details. Latent-reference consistency improves reference fidelity at inference. Our proposed benchmark suite assesses lowoverlap view bridging, long-range generation, and the use of off-trajectory references. Results on diverse benchmarks show the effectiveness of our pipeline. Limitations. Although our method generates high-quality 3D scenes, it may lack fine-detailed and structural geometry. When target views have little visual overlap with the spatial references, these references provide limited guidance, which may reduce generation quality. Further discussion is provided in the supplementary material.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: This supplementary material describes the training and inference procedures for WorldBridge (Sec. A), the construction of the WorldBridge benchmark suite (Sec. B), and the evaluation settings and metrics (Sec. C). We present additional qualitative comparisons and application examples (Sec. D), and discuss limitations and the role of global scene context (Sec. E). A. Implementation Details A.1. Training Configuration We implement WorldBridge based on GAE [52], which provides good geometry-appearance space for scene generation. The scene encoder and scene reader are initialized from LagerNVS [67] and tuned; the reference and text encoders are DepthAnything v3 [47] and Qwen3-0.6B [89] and kept frozen; the RGB and geometry decoder are kept frozen; the pipeline has 0.94B trainable parameters in total. We train our model on collection of video clips from RealEstate10K [103], DL3DV [48], and SpatialVID [72], which contains about 22k video clips at 1280 720 resolution and is separate from the evaluation benchmarks. The training data is labeled by ViPE [28] and DepthAnything v3 [47] for metric camera pose and depth, and Qwen3.527B [58] for caption. The diffusion transformer is trained with resolution of 672 378, while the global context supervision is at resolution of 512 288. The model is trained on 32 GPUs for 10 epochs, using the Adam optimizer with batch size of 64, and learning rate decaying from 5 105 to 5 106. A.2. Training Strategy Target-view sampling. At each training step, we draw the target sequence length uniformly from {21, . . . , 41}. We use two sampling modes to expose the model to both wide camera motion and dense local trajectories. With probability 0.8, we partition the full clip into equal-duration bins and select one valid frame uniformly from each bin. With probability 0.2, we sample consecutive frames, using randomly selected valid start and stride when constantstride sequence is available, and an irregular sequence of valid frames within the same duration range otherwise. In both modes, we order the target frames chronologically and use their sequence indices 0, . . . , 1 for temporal RoPE. Reference-view sampling. Temporal references are selected from the sampled target sequence, while spatial references are drawn uniformly without replacement from the same clips full pool of valid frames after excluding the sampled target frame indices. Visual overlap between spatial references and targets can vary across samples. We sample up to 6 references during training, while it can infer with more references. The temporal-only configurations use the first frame (15%), both endpoints (15%), or three to six target frames (10%). The spatial-only configuration uses one to six spatial references (35%). The mixed configurations use the first frame and one to five spatial references (10%), or both endpoints and one to four spatial references (10%). The remaining 5% of the configuration distribution uses no image references. Within each configuration, any variable reference count is sampled uniformly over its specified range. separate 5% joint dropout of reference, camera, and text conditioning provides the unconditional branch for classifier-free guidance. Temporal position dropout. With probability 0.5, we disable temporal RoPE for temporal references and treat them as spatial references. Target-to-target attention retains temporal RoPE. This exposes the model to the same reference images both with and without temporal positions, complementing training with spatial references, whose interactions always omit temporal RoPE. A.3. Inference Setting For the benchmark results reported in the main paper, we generate each target sequence in single sampling run with 50 denoising steps, classifier-free guidance scale of 2, seed of 42, and an empty text prompt. Let be the number of requested target views. When 41, we insert 41 auxiliary cameras into the target trajectory and generate all 41 views jointly. We evaluate the outputs at the original target cameras. When > 41 (e.g., = 56 for WorldBridge-Long and WorldBridge-Agent (On), and = 50 for WorldBridge-Agent (Off)), we extend the temporal RoPE indices from 0, . . . , 40 to 0, . . . , 1 and generate all views. For longer trajectories, WorldBridge also supports segment-wise generation. The final generated frames of each segment serve as temporal context for generating the next segment. A.4. Latent-reference Consistency Configuration For the implementation of Latent-reference Consistency, we estimate each references metric depth once with MoGe3 [38] using the supplied camera field of view, and single refinement step in each denoising step. Using the supplied cameras, we forward-project the reference RGB into each target view and retain valid projected pixels. The gradient direction is RMS-normalized, with relative step size of 0.01. For view i, let di [0, 1] be its distance to the nearest reference (if the reference is spatial reference, it should be the target view that is nearest to the spatial reference), normalized by the maximum over views. At 10 noise level t, the fresh-noise mixing coefficient is λi(t) = 0.1t + (0.5 0.1t)di, capped at 0.5. Thus, the transition 1 λi mixes estimated and fresh noise with amplitudes and λi, respectively. Inference time. We evaluate the inference efficiency of 41-frame sequence generation on single H200. Under 50 denoising steps, seed 42, and CFG 2, using LRC costs 18.3% more time compared with inference without LRC. B. WorldBridge Benchmark Details Our WorldBridge benchmark suite comprises 100 short real-world video clips, 20 long real-world video clips, and 20 agentic-authored worlds. Each authored world contributes two paired evaluation cases, On and Off, for total of 40 cases. We will release our benchmark as well as our model upon acceptance. Real-video curation and annotation. The curation protocol uses two stages. First, Qwen3.5-27B [58] separately reviews chronological sequence of sampled RGB frames and the candidate reference images. The first review checks shot continuity, distracting overlays, visual quality, and independently moving objects. The second checks whether the references provide complementary observations of coherent scene. RoMa v2 [15] measures matching support for the single Short pair or all 15 Long pairs. The protocol advances candidates to reconstruction when both visual checks and the matching criteria pass. In the second stage, ViPE [28] estimates per-frame camera pose and intrinsics along the retained clip. DA3 Nested [47] uses the estimated cameras and intrinsics to predict the depth maps. One positive scale per clip rescales the ViPE [28] translations to the metric scale of the predicted depth. We check frame correspondence, valid depth coverage, abrupt pose changes, scale consistency across windows, and agreement between overlapping depth estimates. We review RGB, depth, and trajectory overlays and hold clips with unresolved issues. Captions describe the scene and camera motion. B.1. WorldBridge-Short The 100 clips come from RealEstate10K [103] (29 clips), DL3DV [48] (37 clips), and SpatialVID [72] (34 clips). All clips durations are 515 seconds, and the first and last frames provide two references. The retained clips include 36 indoor, 20 outdoor, 23 indoor-to-outdoor, and 21 outdoor-to-indoor paths. We back-project candidate target pixels with the estimated target depth, transform them to each reference camera, and check image bounds and agreement with the reference depth. We take the union of the two reference sup11 port masks. Eligible intermediate frames have at least 50% estimated reference support. Viewpoint diversity and nearduplicate checks reduce repeated views, and we retain at most six targets per clip. This yields 549 target views across 100 clips, with two to six views per clip. B.2. WorldBridge-Long The 20 retained long clips comprise 10 indoor and 10 outdoor scenes. The evaluated spans range from 20 to 60.0 seconds. Six reference frames follow one continuous trajectory and cover complementary regions. We place ten evenly spaced interior timestamps in each of the five reference intervals and use the nearest retained source frames, excluding the references. This gives 50 evaluation views per clip. For labeling the long clips, we sample native frames at approximately 15 fps while preserving the exact six reference frames and their timestamps. We estimate dense depth in overlapping windows and apply single translation scale across the clip. B.3. WorldBridge-Agent World construction. The 20 agent-authored worlds comprise 10 indoor and 10 outdoor environments. Indoor examples include offices, libraries, exhibition spaces, and residences. Outdoor examples include streets, markets, gardens, and coastal trails. We use agent-assisted geometric blockouts to specify the layout, traversable regions, and camera paths. We render structural guides at the reference cameras and use them to generate images with shared scene description and appearance cues. We compare the generated views against the guides and other references, checking openings, major structures, object identity, and plausible sightlines. Off-path camera placement also checks clearance, reachability, and visibility in the blockout. In our construction, the agent is GPT-6 Astra [56], and the image generation model is GPT-Image [57]. Paired On and Off conditions. Both conditions share the same authored world and target trajectory. On-trajectory provides six reference images at poses on the trajectory, with known temporal positions. Off-trajectory provides six separately generated references at poses outside the target path, with spatial camera parameters and no assigned timestamps. We select 50 common target cameras by taking the nearest authored poses to ten evenly spaced interior times in each interval between successive On references. The nominal trajectories span 5058 seconds. The authored camera parameters specify the intended views, and the structural guides constrain reference generation. B.4. Benchmark Visualizations We provide more visualization examples of our WorldBridge benchmark suite in Figs. 6 to 8 to show the diversity Figure 6. More visualizations of WorldBridge-Short samples. of our benchmark. Reference overlap. We report RoMa v2 matching coverage for the reference inputs. For each direction of reference pair, we count pixels with in-bounds forward and backward matches, confidence at least 0.5 in both directions, and round-trip error of at most two pixels on 512 288 grid. We divide by the size of the full source grid and average both directions. There is 1 pair per short clip and 15 pairs per six-reference case. The quantitative results are shown below. C. Discussion E.1. Limitations and Failure Cases WorldBridge can generate convincing RGB views coupled with dense point maps, while its 3D geometry is not perfectly fine-grained. One possible reason is the bottleneck of view-based 3D representation, rather than the 3D native representation. For example, in the office and street examples in Fig. 13, the desktops and building fronts establish the overall layout, but chair frames and the edges of walls break up into sparse or uneven points.
